Its erection at an incline must be positioned in such a way that it corresponds to the description of a Pythagorean right-angled triangle. That is to say, if the length is divided into five parts, the head of the screw should be raised by three of these parts, so that the space from the vertical line to its lower opening is four parts. The final book contains a description of the form and the reasoning behind why this is necessary.

<note>A woodcut illustration of an Archimedean screw (coclea) used for irrigation or drainage. The device consists of a wooden shaft with an internal spiral encased in a cylinder, tilted at an angle. The lower end is submerged in water, and the upper end is supported by a tall wooden pillar (labeled 'b'). A large treadwheel (labeled 'd') is attached to the center of the shaft, allowing humans to turn the device by treading on its rungs. Water is shown being lifted through the screw and discharging from the top into a wooden trough or basin. The letter 'a' labels the main body of the screw.</note>

Regarding the materials from which machines for drawing water are made, the methods by which they are perfected, and the means by which they receive motion to provide infinite utility through their revolutions,

<summary>This passage details the mechanical construction and proper geometric inclination of an Archimedean screw used for water extraction.</summary>
